{"chunk_id":"R2-1816537-001","collection":"ran2_tdoc_chunks","metadata":{"source":["Nokia"],"tdocNumber":"R2-1816537","title":"Assistance information for NR overheating"},"point_id":"7940813722355854466"}
This contribution relates to Email discussion 103bis#16 on NR overheating, that collects suggestions to UE Overheating Assistance Information. It discusses the issues related to roles of the UE and the network with regard to the trigger, control and execution of the identified content of the assistance information. All of the identified potential entries for the UE assistance information due to overheating originate from the assumption that they are the main contributors to the overheating issue, as they are enablers of higher UE throughputs. If certain ‘contributor’ for overheating is selected by the UE, it will be possible to ask for: - reduced number of CC (agreed in RAN2#103bis) - reduced MIMO rank (for UL and DL separately) - reduced BWP width (for UL and DL separately) - PSCell/SCell to be released - reduced aggregated bandwidth across all carriers - FR indication to be released Even though, the UE assistance information is intended to be a “suggestion” for the network, it is essential for network to understand the UE decision to ensure that NR overheating information is practically usable in the future. There will be differences for needed function between the suggestion given by the UE and the network action. The effect will not depend solely on what is defined as possible report but also how reliably the assistance information can be taken by the network. Thus, the settings of the above entries (if agreed) should be clarified. There are two obvious and tied decisive factors to set the UE assistance information:

{"chunk_id":"R2-2111528-010","collection":"ran2_tdoc_chunks","metadata":{"source":["Xiaomi"],"tdocNumber":"R2-2111528","title":"Summary of [AT116-e][036][ePowSav] RLM/BFD relaxation (Xiaomi)"},"point_id":"1803923782563033012"}
Referring to Rel-16 RRM relaxation, there are some misunderstanding between RAN2 and RAN4 as some criteria and relaxed methods are put into both RAN2 and RAN4 specification. Therefore rapporteur thinks we can make the responsibility more clearly. Three companies[4][5][8] mentioned this part. With this relaxation procedure, one way is that RAN4 specification should capture the relaxed methods as well as the corresponding requirements for RLM/BFD relaxation, while RAN2 specification should capture the relaxation criteria as well as the RRC configurations. Rapporteur also wants to remind that RLM is handled by RRC layer while BFD is handle by MAC layer. So furthermore RAN2 can capture RLM relaxation criteria in RRC aspect (i.e. TS 38.331) and BFD relaxation criteria in MAC aspect (i.e. TS 38.321). However there is still argument[8] that the relaxed RLM/BFD criterion are discussed in RAN4 and captured in 38.133. Anyway rapporteur think we can proposal a suggestion as way forward. Proposal: The relaxation methods as well as the corresponding requirements for RLM/BFD relaxation should be captured in RAN4 specification, while the criteria as well as the configurations should be captured in RAN2 specification(e.g. RLM captured in TS 38.331 and BFD captured in TS 38.321). Q8: Do companies agree with the above proposal and if not, please provide your suggested change? Summary: Majorities do not agree that the relaxation criteria should be captured in RAN2 specifications, and think only configuration and capability of RLM/BFD relaxation can be captured in RAN2. However since RAN4 is being discussing the details about RLM/BFD relaxation. Therefore rapporteur think we can wait for RAN4 progress. Proposal: None Once RAN2 has reached some agreements, rapporteur wonders whether to provide our suggestions to RAN4 as a reference for future work. Q9: Do companies agree to send an LS about our RAN2 suggestions to RAN4 as a reference for future work? Summary: It seems that currently we don’t have serious issues that needs to inform of RAN4, therefore maybe an LS is not needed. Proposal: None If companies raise some issues which are not mentioned in this contribution, please provide your opinions here.

{"chunk_id":"R2-2102966-003","collection":"ran2_tdoc_chunks","metadata":{"source":["Ericsson"],"tdocNumber":"R2-2102966","title":"Mechanisms for RRM relaxation for RedCap"},"point_id":"4463364104949036229"}
When an NR device is in RRC_IDLE/INACTIVE the main contributors to power consumption are activities related to loop convergence (automatic gain control (AGC)/automatic frequency control (AFC)/Timing), RRM measurements, paging monitoring, and potential cell reselections. Part of this loop is up to implementation and therefore not specified in detail. There are contributors not included here, such as periodical connections to the NW for the sake of registration updates, as they are quite infrequent. In-between occasions for the abovementioned activities, the device can enjoy various levels of power saving. The figure below depicts an example of typical RRC_IDLE/INACTIVE device activities and accommodated level of power consumption when camping on a cell. Figure 1. Principle of loop convergence measurements (without neighbor RRM, SI reading, registration updates, etc). The loop convergence related measurements, i.e. AGC, time and frequency tracking loops (TTL & FTL), are necessary for the sake of paging reception. This means one SSB for AGC (depending on time since last AGC) every now and then (say every 160..300 ms) and one for combined AFC/measurements. Note that, only serving cell related activities are depicted, i.e. no neighbor RRM, no SI reading, no registration updates. This scenario is the best that can be achieved (i.e. minimum amount of activities) in terms of power saving, i.e. if the device can refrain from neighbor cell RRM measurements.

ered, RAN2 can start ASN.1 review early and have more than 3 weeks for 1st round ASN.1 review. This gives RAN2 sufficient time to make sure a high-quality 1st round ASN.1 review, where companies can have a comprehensive review and RIL issue identification. During offline discussion in RAN2 #129bis meeting, some companies have questions on whether merging RRC specification in RAN2 level is feasible or not. We observe that it is not the first time we have a temporary merged specification in RAN2: During LTE time, RAN2 RRC specification rapporteur merged a temporary RRC spec for ASN.1 review During NR time, RAN2 UE capability rapporteur merges two temporary specification (38.306 and 38.331 Section 6.3.3) for merged CR review Observation 3: RAN2 already have two examples of temporary specification generated by RAN2 specification rapporteur: 1) LTE RRC specification 2) NR UE capability specification (38.306 and 38.331 section 6.3.3). The above examples prove that it is possible to merge a temporary specification from RAN2 level before plenary. Furthermore, there are some further questions on whether MCC would have enough time to do an early implementation or not. Note that, the above two examples of temporary specifications are all merged by specification rapporteur. Therefore, in our understanding, if MCC doesn’t have enough time to do early implementation, either specification rapporteur or volunteered RAN2 companies can take this responsibility. Observation 4: Either RRC specification rapporteur or volunteered RAN2 company can take the responsibility to merge temporary RRC specification for ASN.1 review. Having merged temporary specification can significantly provide more ASN.1 review time for RAN2, especially for cross-WI RIL issues. Note that, during Rel-18, many cross-WI RIL issues are identified and resolving cross-WI RIL issues usually take more than 1 WG meeting. In Rel-19, we foresee several cross-WI items might need RAN2 to take more time to review and discuss. For example, AI/ML air beam management/CSI prediction vs. MIMO enhancement. Those cross-WI ASN.1 review can greatly benefit from this merged temporary specification for early review. Based on above discussion, we would like to propose below Rel-19 ASN.1 review timeline: Proposal 1: RAN2 endorse the below Rel-19 ASN.1 review timeline: After RAN2 WG meeting, RAN2 start RRC running CR review and endorse. RAN2 merge temporary RRC spec (by MCC or RRC specification rapporteur or volunteered RAN2 company), meanwhile, RAN2 start per WI ASN.1 review based on endorsed per WI RRC CR. After merged temporary RRC spec is ready, RAN2 start cross-WI ASN.1 review and continue per WI ASN.1 review based on merged temporary RRC spec. (1st ASN.1 review is around 3-4 weeks, 2nd ASN.1 review is around 2 weeks) RIL discussion paper submitted to RAN2 #131bis meeting, deadline is expected at Wednesday before the meeting week. RAN2 repeat the same procedure for 2nd round ASN.1 review after RAN2 #131bis meeting.

{"chunk_id":"R2-1816511-002","collection":"ran2_tdoc_chunks","metadata":{"source":["MediaTek"],"tdocNumber":"R2-1816511","title":"RRC buffer size restriction"},"point_id":"2770529302662891283"}
During previous RAN2 meetings, RAN2 identified the over-sized IEs including RACH-ConfigDedicated, MeasObjectNR, CSI-MeasConfig, BWP-Downlink and BWP-Uplink. The main contributors to the size of each IE is highlighted in Table 1. The total RRC configuration size scales up based on the number of configured serving cells and BWPs. Table 1- Main contributors to the over-sized IE and total RRC configuration Based on our previous evaluation, the size of RACH-ConfigDedicated would be ~1Kbytes if number of CSI-RS resources is 16 and number of RA occasions per CSI-RS is 8. The size of MeasObjectNR is ~500bytes if CSI-RS resource is not configured. The size of CSI-MeasConfig is ~7Kbytes if 100 CSI-RS resources are configured per carrier without non-PMI feedback. Although the assumed number for CSI-RS resources are large, it is observed that the size of CSI-MeasConfig increase slightly if more CSI-RS resources are configured. If 4 serving cells are configured, the total RRC configuration would be ~42Kbytes. Compared with other IEs, the size of CSI-MeasConfig is the dominant factor to the overall configuration. RAN1 should further consider to reduce the size of CSI-MeasConfig if the flexibility to configure many carriers and BWPs is intended to be supported. Observation 1: RAN1 should consider to reduce the size of CSI-MeasConfig if large number of carriers e.g. 8 are intended to be supported. Up to 2 BWPs per carrier and up to 8 carriers are assumed in Rel-15 for total RRC configuration evaluation. Considering both bandwidth adaptation and carrier aggregation are tools for the network to utilize the frequency spectrum, it is not expected that many carriers with more than one BWPs per each carrier are configured simultaneously. Although RAN1 feedback on the typical configurations for the above parameters has not been received, the network can restriction the total configuration to 45Kbytes by leveraging the values of those physical layer parameters, number of BWPs and number of carriers. Observation 2: The network can restrict the size of overall configuration to 45Kbytes by leveraging the values of the physical layer parameters, number of BWPs and the number of carriers.

nfigCommon. The NR SIB1 size can vary a lot normally ranges from 233 to 614 bytes, excluding headers, depending on configuration. Whether the SIB1 size is critical, may depend on different network implementations based on the subset of features activated as well as network deployments e.g. availability of bandwidth. Basically, it is important to understand the SIB1 component and analyze which parts of SIB1 contribute heavily to the size, since the contribution is highly uneven across IE groups. The main contributors are typically PLMN / cell access related info: If multiple PLMNs are configured, PLMN could consume a sizeable space and become one of the largest contributors to SIB1 size. The main driver is the number of configured PLMNs together with related identity and access information, thus, it would be a potential candidate to look into. UAC: UAC provides details on the cell access related information also a big contributor in SIB1 size. In 5G-SIB1, this information has been designed to be very flexible. It allows defining multiple barring configurations per-PLMN and per-category granularity and allows extensions to access categories. UAC requirements are defined by SA1 and as indicated in the ongoing TR22.870, SA1 is anticipated to introduce new services for 6G. This may likely define new access categories to manage associated access attempts. Therefore, SIB1 design must consider this potential extension to access categories when analyzing its contents and size. The main size drivers are the number of access categories, the number of PLMNs, and the number of barring sets. Scheduling Information: The scheduling information provide detail information on how/when SIBs are scheduled and the SIB mapping. Since SIB1 governs the timing of all SIBs, introducing more SIBs would gradually increase the size of scheduling information and in turn the size of SIB1. The design of 5G-SIB1 is such that whenever anything is changed within SIB1 it forces NW to change whole SIB1 and UEs to acquire that. The other aspect is introduction of multiple SIBs may potentially also impact the number of SI change indications, which in turn may force UE to read SIB1 updates more often irrespective of whether or not the UE is required to read the updated SI. It is inevitable that with every release there would be newer SIBs introduced, but whether the impact to SIB1 can be minimized is to be investigated. Serving Cell Configuration: The serving cell configuration carries many NR DL/UL common configurations. The DL common config is always present in SIB1, however, the UL config common is optional in SIB1. The DL parameters (SSB pattern, TDD config, DL BWP size) contribute significantly but they do not scale much and stay stable. However, UL parameters grow substantially when RACH patterns, multiple UL BWPs, or SUL are configured. This means UL config will likely grow faster than DL config in 6G evolution. By contrast, some other SIB1 fields such as cell selection thresholds, connection establishment, failure control, UE timers/constants, and emergency support flags are comparatively small or often fixed, even though they remain important for their respective procedures. Feature- or deployment-specific items are also conditional and may only be essential for certain UE types or scenarios.

will only have 1 week (or 2 days for the worst case) for 1st round ASN.1 review, which is impossible for companies to identify and submit RIL issues for further discussion. Observation 2: If temporary RRC specification is considered, RAN2 can start ASN.1 review early and have more than 3 weeks for 1st round ASN.1 review. This gives RAN2 sufficient time to make sure a high-quality 1st round ASN.1 review, where companies can have a comprehensive review and RIL issue identification. Observation 3: RAN2 already have two examples of temporary specification generated by RAN2 specification rapporteur: 1) LTE RRC specification 2) NR UE capability specification (38.306 and 38.331 section 6.3.3). Observation 4: Either RRC specification rapporteur or volunteered RAN2 company can take the responsibility to merge temporary RRC specification for ASN.1 review. Proposal 1: RAN2 endorse the below Rel-19 ASN.1 review timeline: After RAN2 WG meeting, RAN2 start RRC running CR review and endorse. RAN2 merge temporary RRC spec (by MCC or RRC specification rapporteur or volunteered RAN2 company), meanwhile, RAN2 start per WI ASN.1 review based on endorsed per WI RRC CR. After merged temporary RRC spec is ready, RAN2 start cross-WI ASN.1 review and continue per WI ASN.1 review based on merged temporary RRC spec. (1st ASN.1 review is around 3-4 weeks, 2nd ASN.1 review is around 2 weeks) RIL discussion paper submitted to RAN2 #131bis meeting, deadline is expected at Wednesday before the meeting week. RAN2 repeat the same procedure for 2nd round ASN.1 review after RAN2 #131bis meeting. Proposal 2: RAN2 to use a WORD/EXCEL document with unique quoting to the original context in the specification as review file to collect companies’ comment, which is a separate file from RRC specification. Proposal 3: The separate review file should be per WI (including cross-WI) per company.

The identified use case that originally justified the need for Rel-14 technical enhancement was exceptional generation of UE’s heat that can lead to hardware multifunction, damage of battery/device and generally to degradation of performance [2]. Even though such a problem is known and can be handled by proper terminal design implementation, RAN2 agreed to work out a standardized solution that would help to diminish device’s thermal issues under condition the overheat detection is due to pure radio configurations contributors, such as high rank MIMO transmissions and high number of carrier aggregations. There was identified match with more generic use cases and potential solutions in [1] and [2] assumed the UE could initiate and change dynamically radio capability. The causation of such UE capabilities temporary change covered variety of reasons [2], including: general UE wish, any/subjective “overaheat”, low battery level, hardware sharing, long term using high performance. In our understanding, the flexibility given to a potential trigger of UE assistance information was eliminated, though. Observation 1: The flexibility given to a potential trigger of UE assistance information for a configuration change was eliminated in RAN2#97bis.
